blocks.text: You just learned merge and join, pandas tools for combining DataFrames based on matching keys, the same way a SQL join looks up a customer id in one table and finds their orders in another. Concat works nothing like that. It does not look at any key column at all. It just glues DataFrames together, end to end, the same way you would tape two spreadsheets one after another or side by side. If merge and join are about relationships between tables, concat is about assembly.

items: Combining January, February, and March sales exports into one full quarter of data.
Stacking prediction batches that came back from a model in separate chunks.
Appending freshly scraped rows onto a dataset you already collected yesterday.
Putting a training split and a validation split back together after you are done inspecting them separately.

blocks.title: The core difference from merge and join
blocks.content: Merge and join ask a question first: which rows in DataFrame A match which rows in DataFrame B. Concat does not ask anything. You hand it a list of DataFrames and it stacks them in exactly the order you gave it. No matching, no lookup, just assembly.

blocks.caption: Concat glues DataFrames together. Merge and join match rows on a key. Very different jobs.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442269794-238421469.png
1. What Concat Actually Does

pd.concat() takes a list of DataFrames and glues them into one. The most common shape you will use looks like pd.concat([df1, df2, df3]). By default it stacks rows on top of each other, treating every DataFrame in the list as another chunk of the same table.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Parameter","Default","What it controls"],"rows":[["objs","required","The list of DataFrames or Series to glue together"],["axis","0","Stack rows on top of each other, or place columns side by side"],["join","outer","Keep every column from every DataFrame, or only the ones they share"],["ignore_index","False","Whether to build a fresh continuous row index or keep the original ones"],["keys","None","Tag every row with a label so you can trace it back to its source DataFrame"]]}

blocks.text: Every one of those parameters matters more than it looks at first glance, and getting the defaults wrong is exactly how quiet bugs sneak into a pipeline. The rest of this lesson works through each one with a real example.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df1 = pd.DataFrame({'product': ['A', 'B'], 'units_sold': [10, 15]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'product': ['C', 'D'], 'units_sold': [8, 20]})

combined = pd.concat([df1, df2])
print(combined)

blocks.title: Order matters, matching does not
blocks.content: Concat has no idea what your columns mean. It just lines things up by column name or by index, depending on the axis. Feed it DataFrames in the wrong order and it will happily glue them together wrong, without a single warning.

blocks.text: 2. Two Directions to Glue: Axis 0 and Axis 1

Concat can glue DataFrames in two directions. Axis 0, the default, stacks rows on top of each other. Axis 1 places DataFrames side by side, lining them up by their shared index instead of stacking rows.
2.1 Axis 0: Stacking Rows on Top of Each Other

This is the version you will use constantly. Axis 0 treats every DataFrame you pass in as more rows for the same table, as long as they share the same columns. Think of taking one spreadsheet, then literally continuing to type more rows underneath the last one, except the new rows came from a second file.

blocks.alt: Axis 0: Stacking Rows on Top of Each Other
blocks.caption: Axis 0, the default, stacks rows on top of each other.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442269794-111825533.png

code.content:
import pandas as pd

week1 = pd.DataFrame({'day': ['Mon', 'Tue'], 'visitors': [230, 190]})
week2 = pd.DataFrame({'day': ['Mon', 'Tue'], 'visitors': [255, 210]})

stacked = pd.concat([week1, week2])
print(stacked)
print(stacked.shape)   # 4 rows, 2 columns

blocks.text: Four rows came out of two DataFrames that had two rows each, because axis 0 is the default and pandas just stacked one on top of the other.
2.2 Axis 1: Placing DataFrames Side by Side

Axis 1 is a different job entirely. Instead of stacking rows, it glues columns together, matching them up using the row index each DataFrame already has. This only makes sense when the DataFrames you are combining share the same index, meaning row 0 in one really does correspond to row 0 in the other.

blocks.alt: Axis 1: Placing DataFrames Side by Side
blocks.caption: Axis 1 places DataFrames side by side, lining columns up by index.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442269794-868310571.png

code.content:
import pandas as pd

product_names = pd.DataFrame({'product': ['Widget A', 'Widget B', 'Widget C']})
unit_prices = pd.DataFrame({'unit_price': [10.0, 12.5, 9.0]})

side_by_side = pd.concat([product_names, unit_prices], axis=1)
print(side_by_side)

blocks.title: Axis 1 trusts the index completely
blocks.content: If the two DataFrames do not share the same index, axis 1 will still run, but it lines rows up by index label, not by position, and any index that only exists in one DataFrame ends up with NaN in the columns from the other. Reset or align the index first if you are not sure they match.

blocks.text: 3. Worked Example: Stacking Three Months of Sales
Here is the version of concat you will reach for the most: taking several monthly exports that all share the exact same columns and gluing them into one continuous dataset.

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Stacking Three Months of Sales
blocks.caption: Three monthly DataFrames with identical columns, stacked into one.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270132-71405985.png
Nine rows, three from each month, all with the same three columns. That is the whole job concat does here: no lookups, no matching, just three tables laid end to end into one.
4. The ignore_index Parameter
There is a catch hiding in that last example, and it is one of the most common concat mistakes beginners make.
4.1 The Repeated Index Gotcha

Look closely at the row index of q1_sales from the example above. jan_sales had rows labeled 0, 1, 2. feb_sales also had rows labeled 0, 1, 2. mar_sales too. Concat does not renumber anything by default, so the combined DataFrame ends up with the index 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, three separate rows all sharing the label 0, three more all sharing the label 1, and so on.

blocks.caption: Without ignore_index, the row index repeats from each source DataFrame.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270134-977517868.png

code.content:
print(q1_sales.index.tolist())
# [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2]

print(q1_sales.loc[0])
# returns THREE rows, not one, because the label 0 appears three times

blocks.title: Why this actually bites people
blocks.content: Anything that relies on the index being unique breaks quietly here. q1_sales.loc[0] returns three rows instead of one. Merging this DataFrame with another one on its index can multiply rows in ways you did not expect. The index still works, it is just no longer a reliable way to point at a single row.

blocks.text: 4.2 Fixing It with ignore_index True
The fix is one keyword argument. ignore_index=True tells concat to throw away the original index from every source DataFrame and build one fresh, continuous index for the combined result.

blocks.caption: With ignore_index True, pandas builds one fresh continuous index.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270134-176847669.png

code.content:
q1_sales = pd.concat([jan_sales, feb_sales, mar_sales], ignore_index=True)
print(q1_sales.index.tolist())
# [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]

blocks.text: This is why you will almost always want ignore_index=True when you are stacking rows with concat. There are rare cases where you want to keep the original index on purpose, usually when you plan to use keys instead to track where each row came from, which is exactly what section 6 covers. But as a default habit, set it to True.
5. When Columns Do Not Match

So far every example has used DataFrames with identical columns. Real monthly exports are rarely that tidy. One file is missing a column, another has an extra one somebody added halfway through the quarter. Concat still runs when this happens, and understanding exactly what it does is important.
5.1 The Default Outer Join Fills Gaps With NaN

By default, concat uses join='outer'. That means it keeps the union of every column across all the DataFrames you are combining. Any row that came from a DataFrame missing one of those columns gets NaN in that spot instead.

blocks.alt: The Default Outer Join Fills Gaps With NaN
blocks.caption: The default outer join keeps every column and fills gaps with NaN.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270135-173989813.png

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df_a = pd.DataFrame({'product': ['A', 'B'], 'units_sold': [10, 15]})
df_b = pd.DataFrame({'product': ['C', 'D'], 'units_sold': [8, 20], 'promo_code': ['SPRING', 'SPRING']})

combined = pd.concat([df_a, df_b], ignore_index=True)
print(combined)
#   product  units_sold promo_code
# 0       A          10        NaN
# 1       B          15        NaN
# 2       C           8     SPRING
# 3       D          20     SPRING

blocks.title: Useful, but easy to miss
blocks.content: Filling gaps with NaN instead of raising an error is genuinely convenient when you expect the mismatch, like a promo code that only applies to certain rows. The problem is when you did not expect it. A typo in a column name, like Units_Sold instead of units_sold, will not throw an error either. It just quietly creates a second column full of NaN. Always check df.columns after a concat if the source files were not guaranteed to be identical.

blocks.text: 5.2 The join Parameter: Outer Versus Inner

join controls exactly how concat handles that mismatch. outer, the default, keeps every column from every DataFrame. inner keeps only the columns that are present in all of them, dropping the rest entirely.

blocks.alt: The join Parameter: Outer Versus Inner
blocks.caption: join equals inner drops any column that is not present in every DataFrame.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270135-247012070.png

blocks.content: {"headers":["join value","What it keeps","What happens to unmatched columns"],"rows":[["outer, the default","The union of all columns from every DataFrame","Filled with NaN wherever a source DataFrame did not have that column"],["inner","Only columns present in every DataFrame being combined","Dropped completely, they never appear in the result"]]}

code.content:
inner_combined = pd.concat([df_a, df_b], join='inner', ignore_index=True)
print(inner_combined)
#   product  units_sold
# 0       A          10
# 1       B          15
# 2       C           8
# 3       D          20

blocks.text: Notice promo_code is gone entirely from the inner join result, not filled with NaN, just gone. Reach for inner when you specifically want a clean DataFrame with no gaps and you are fine losing any column that not every source shares.
6. Tagging Rows With the keys Parameter

Once you set ignore_index=True, you lose any trace of which source DataFrame a given row came from. Most of the time that is fine. Sometimes you need to keep that information around, for debugging or for reporting back which month a strange value showed up in. That is what keys is for.

blocks.alt: Tagging Rows With the keys Parameter
blocks.caption: The keys parameter tags every row with its original DataFrame.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270136-793814522.png

code.content:
q1_tagged = pd.concat(
    [jan_sales, feb_sales, mar_sales],
    keys=['jan', 'feb', 'mar']
)
print(q1_tagged.loc['feb'])
#   product  units_sold  revenue
# 0 Widget A         140     1400
# 1 Widget B          90      900
# 2 Widget C          75      750

blocks.text: keys builds a hierarchical index, sometimes called a MultiIndex, where the outer level is whatever label you gave each DataFrame and the inner level is that DataFrame's original row index. You can slice straight into one source with q1_tagged.loc['feb'], or you can keep the whole combined DataFrame and still know exactly where every row came from.

blocks.title: You can drop the hierarchy later
blocks.content: If you only needed keys temporarily, for debugging or for a one time check, call q1_tagged.reset_index(level=0).rename(columns={'level_0': 'source_month'}) to turn that outer label into a normal column instead of an index level.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Monthly Sales Files With a Missing promo_code Column

Let's put outer join and a real gotcha together in one example. Say only the January sales file has a promo_code column, because that is the only month a promotion ran. February and March never had one.

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Monthly Sales Files With a Missing promo_code Column
blocks.caption: One month has an extra promo_code column, so the other months end up with NaN in that column.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270136-955539346.png

The result has nine rows and a promo_code column, because the default outer join kept it. But that column only has real values for the three January rows, and even one of those was already empty. Every single row from February and March shows NaN in promo_code, six rows worth, plus the one Widget B row from January that never had a promo code either.

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Monthly Sales Files With a Missing promo_code Column
blocks.caption: A quick isna sum check catches exactly which column and how many rows have the gap.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442270136-131962313.png

blocks.title: Make isna a habit after every concat with uncertain columns
blocks.content: Seven missing values out of nine rows is easy to miss just by eyeballing a printed DataFrame, especially once it grows past a handful of rows. Running col.isna().sum() right after a concat, on any column you are not sure every source DataFrame had, takes one line and catches exactly this kind of silent gap before it reaches anything downstream.

blocks.text: 8. Quick Reference

blocks.content: {"headers":["Tool","What it matches on","Typical use"],"rows":[["concat","Nothing, just position or index order","Stacking DataFrames with the same shape, like monthly exports"],["merge","Values in a shared key column","Combining two tables based on a relationship, like customers and orders"],["join","The DataFrame index","Combining two DataFrames that already share an index"]]}

items: Default to axis=0 for stacking rows and reach for axis=1 only when you truly need to glue columns together by index.
Set ignore_index=True almost every time you stack rows, unless you specifically need the original index preserved.
Remember the default join is outer, which fills gaps with NaN instead of raising an error, so mismatched columns can slip through silently.
Use join='inner' when you want a clean result with no NaN gaps and can afford to drop columns that are not shared.
Reach for keys when you need to trace a row back to the DataFrame it came from.

blocks.text: Concat is the simplest of the three combining tools in pandas, and that simplicity is exactly what makes it easy to misuse. It will not warn you about a typo in a column name or a forgotten ignore_index. Get in the habit of checking shape, columns, and isna sum right after every concat, and it becomes one of the safest tools in your pandas toolkit instead of one of the sneakiest. Next up is groupby, where you will start summarizing the rows you just combined.
